title: Live with them in kindness
hook: live with your wives in kindness, even when you dislike something (4:19)

segments.voice: Yesterday, mirath: the shares, set out by name, after debts are paid. Your line was everyone has a share. Did you write down where your things should go? Day three hundred seventy-nine.

It's the dishes. Or the way they load the dishwasher. Or the phone at dinner, the late replies, the thing they always say at family gatherings. Anyone who has shared a home with someone for long enough has a list. Most of the items are small. Some aren't. And the list has a way of growing louder than everything else about the person. An-Nisa has a verse for exactly that moment, and it's one of the most practical lines in the Qur'an.
screen: `IT'S THE DISHES.` → `EVERYONE HAS A LIST.` → `THE LIST GETS LOUDER.`

segments.voice: Verse 19 starts by forbidding something that commentators say was done in Arabia before Islam: when a man died, his heirs could treat his widow as part of the estate, and control whom she married. The verse says no: it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will, and don't press them to give back what you gave them. Then it turns to marriage itself. In Pickthall's words: "But consort with them in kindness, for if ye hate them it may happen that ye hate a thing wherein Allah hath placed much good." The Arabic is 'ashiruhunna bil-ma'ruf. 'Ashara means to live together closely, to be companions. Bil-ma'ruf, with the good that everyone recognizes, the same ma'ruf we met in calling to good. Not a special religious kindness: the ordinary decency any neighbor would know. Then the surprise: if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike something in which God has placed much good. The verse expects dislike. It doesn't pretend a marriage is free of it. A hadith in Sahih Muslim puts it in household terms: a believing man should not hate a believing woman; if he dislikes one trait in her, he will be pleased with another. And a hadith in Tirmidhi reports the Prophet ﷺ saying: the best of you are the best to their families, and I am the best of you to my family. Commentators apply the principle of this verse to both spouses. The list is real. The verse simply asks you to keep reading past it, to the good that's on the other page.
screen: `NOT INHERITED AGAINST THEIR WILL` · `'ASHIRU: LIVE CLOSE, AS COMPANIONS` · `DISLIKE, AND MUCH GOOD IN IT` · `THE BEST OF YOU TO YOUR FAMILY` · then, large: `CONSORT WITH THEM IN KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: When the bell starts, think of someone you live with, or someone close: a spouse, a parent, a roommate, a sibling. Let one complaint about them come up. Don't push it away; it's real. Now, alongside it, find one good thing in them, something you'd miss if they were gone. Then a second. Let the good things sit next to the complaint until the complaint is no longer the only thing in the room. Choose one small kindness you'll do for them today. The bell holds the time.
Live with them in kindness. 'Ashiruhunna bil-ma'ruf, from 4:19: even when you dislike something, there may be much good in it. Today's word.
screen: `LIVE WITH THEM IN KINDNESS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: kindness at home. Today, do that one small kindness for the person on your list, without mentioning the complaint. Day three hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims cite 4:19 and the hadith 'the best of you are the best to their families' in marriage sermons and counseling, as the basis for treating a spouse with recognized kindness and fairness.

original.note: Arabic: and live with them in kindness, with the recognized good (4:19).

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to your wife.
what it means: live as close companions with recognized kindness, and look for the good even in what you dislike.
what a scholar hears: the verse first ends a pre-Islamic practice of inheriting widows; 'ashara, intimate companionship; ma'ruf, the customary good.
